title: Question 1.4
statement_text: What is the smallest possible exponent $C_{p,k}$ for which the following theorem is true: let $k\geq 3$, $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $\delta=\varepsilon^{C_{p,k}}$; then for any $X_1,\dots,X_k\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p^n$, at least one of the following holds: the number of $k$-cycles $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in X_1\times \dots\times X_k$ is at least $\delta N^{k-1}$, or we can delete less than $\varepsilon N$ elements from each of the sets $X_1,\dots,X_k$ so that afterwards no $k$-cycles remain?
context_text: Throughout, $p\geq 2$ is a fixed prime, $n$ is arbitrary and $N=|\mathbb{F}_p^n|=p^n$. Given sets $X_1,\dots,X_k\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n$, a $k$-cycle is a $k$-tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in X_1\times\dots\times X_k$ with $x_1+\dots+x_k=0$. This is the arithmetic $k$-cycle removal lemma of Green (proved for all finite abelian groups with tower-type bounds); the question is about the best polynomial dependence of $\delta$ on $\varepsilon$ when the group is $\mathbb{F}_p^n$. For $k\geq 3$ let $0<c_{p,k}<1$ be defined by $\inf_{0<t<1}\frac{t^0+t^1+\dots+t^{p-1}}{t^{(p-1)/k}}=p^{1-c_{p,k}}$. For $k=3$, Fox and Lovász proved the statement with exponent $C_{p,3}=1+\frac{1}{c_{p,3}}=\Theta(\log p)$, and this exponent is optimal for $k=3$. The paper proves the statement for every $k\geq 3$ with exponent $C_{p,k}=(k-2)(C_{p,3}-1)+1=\frac{k-2}{c_{p,3}}+1$, and shows via constructions of $k$-colored sum-free sets that the smallest possible exponent must be at least $\frac{k-2}{c_{p,k}}+1$. The achieved exponent is within a factor of $O(\log p)$ from this lower bound (independently of $k$), but the exact optimum remains open.
notes: PDF source — math may be garbled; the exponent expressions involve infimum definitions of constants $c_{p,k}$ and $c_{p,3}$ that appear clean in context.
paper_title: A polynomial bound for the arithmetic $k$-cycle removal lemma in vector spaces
